title: Microdrama Platform FlareFlow Sets Thailand Launch on AIS Play (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Microdrama platform FlareFlow will launch in Thailand on Nov. 2 through AIS Play, the entertainment service of Thai telecom operator Advanced Info
body:
Microdrama platform FlareFlow will launch in Thailand on Nov. 2 through AIS Play, the entertainment service of Thai telecom operator Advanced Info Service (AIS), in a deal brokered by Singapore-based distributor Rock Networks.

	FlareFlow, the vertical video service owned by COL Group, will cost subscribers THB39 ($1.15) a month. AIS Play users will find a branded FlareFlow section stocked with curated English-, Chinese- and Korean-language series, every one of them carrying Thai subtitles.
	

	Romance, drama, fantasy and reality shows feature in the lineup, alongside a selection of LGBTQ+ titles.

	Launch titles include the English-language “From Janitor to Mrs Billionaire,” the Chinese-language “Rise of Aurora’s Fallen General” and the Korean Boys’ Love series “My Team Leader Is Working Late Again.” Also on the slate is “SupermodelMe: Make It or Break It,” a reality contest franchise shot in vertical format and fronted by Thai TV personality, actor and model Cindy Bishop.

	“Thailand is one of Southeast Asia’s most creative, connected and culturally influential entertainment markets,” said Timothy Oh, general manager of COL Group International and chief marketing officer of FlareFlow. “Our launch with AIS Play is about making premium vertical entertainment accessible to more Thai audiences. At THB39 per month, viewers will be able to discover thousands of mobile-first stories backed by the scale, content library and industry experience of COL Group.”

	“It is also an opportunity to introduce Thai audiences to a broader range of stories, genres and creative perspectives from around the world, while building a foundation for future collaboration with Thailand’s creators, producers and entertainment industry.”
	

	Rock Networks, FlareFlow’s exclusive partner for telco and OTT integration across Asia, negotiated the commercial terms with AIS. The Singapore-headquartered company will also run the relationship for FlareFlow, handling integration, the launch itself and co-marketing.

	“AIS Play is the right home for FlareFlow’s launch in Thailand,” said Beatrice Lee, CEO of Rock Networks. “Our role is to match world-class content with the region’s leading telcos and platforms, and this partnership brings a global microdrama leader to one of Thailand’s largest customer bases. Thailand is the first of several markets where we’ll be bringing FlareFlow to telco and OTT partners across Asia.”

	COL Group was among the early movers in microdramas in both China and the U.S. FlareFlow has released more than 5,000 series to date, supports 14 languages and claims upward of 50 million registered users in over 200 countries and territories.

	The Thai rollout forms part of what the company calls its Vertical 2.0 strategy. The plan is to push the format past standard microdramas with higher production values, a wider spread of genres and new formats such as reality, documentary and drama.

	AIS and FlareFlow also plan to look beyond distribution. The two sides will explore Thai content development, work with local creators, localization and new mobile entertainment formats for Thailand and the wider Southeast Asian region.

	AIS counted 53.9 million customers across its businesses as of June 2026. That includes 47.1 million subscribers on its 5G mobile network and 5.3 million on its fixed broadband service, AIS 3BB Fibre3. Microdrama platform ReelShort entered Southeast Asia through a partnership with AIS in April.

schema.headline: Microdrama Platform FlareFlow Sets Thailand Launch on AIS Play (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘American History X’ Director Tony Kaye Takes On Leicester’s Giant Monsters in Short ‘Will You Still Love Me Tomorrow?’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Tony Kaye, the British director of “American History X” and “Detachment,” will direct “Will You Still Love Me Tomorrow?,” a short running five minu
body:
Tony Kaye, the British director of “American History X” and “Detachment,” will direct “Will You Still Love Me Tomorrow?,” a short running five minutes that blends documentary with reality drama and plays out among the giant monster sculptures installed across Leicester, England.

	Hiu Man Chan, a film entrepreneur and academic in creative industries at De Montfort University, is producing. The project will pair Kaye with up-and-coming actors and filmmakers from the university and Leicester’s wider creative scene, and the production is taking an experimental, collaborative route.
	

	The narrative will take shape around the chosen cast and participants, with the camera catching chance encounters and real human experiences as the film asks whether people can come to understand and love each other across their differences. The shoot commences on Friday. Louis Lingjaerde (“Vipers”) is the cinematographer.

	The short will take its setting from Leicester Monsters, a downtown program run by BID Leicester that has placed oversized creatures on the city’s streets and in its public spaces to coax visitors into exploring the center. Bristol-based Designs in Air installed the monsters.

	“Forty years ago, I made a commercial for solid fuel in which a dog, a cat and a mouse kissed each other in front of a real coal fire, to the music of ‘Will You Still Love Me Tomorrow.’ I’ve never forgotten that image,” Kaye said. “Now, with the Leicester Monsters movie, I find myself returning to the same idea. Perhaps the universe is the real coal fire, and we are all just animals gathered around it, trying to work out how to love one another. The question is as simple as it is impossible: how can we all get along, forever?”
	

	Leicester is often described as one of the most diverse cities in the U.K. The film will use that mix, with giant creatures popping up around town as a surreal backdrop, to probe the pull between difference and belonging, and between freedom and commitment.

	“I am passionate about the most important human feeling – love – in storytelling, as well as packaging unique projects like this to challenge conventional filmmaking. I look forward to this creative journey with Tony, one of Britain’s greatest talents, and to put the city of Leicester in motion,” Chan said.

	Kaye’s first feature, 1998’s “American History X,” tackled racism and redemption and earned Edward Norton an Oscar nomination for best actor. His 2011 film “Detachment,” starring Adrien Brody, took two prizes at the Deauville American Film Festival – the Critics’ Award and the Revelation Prize – and won the Tokyo International Film Festival’s Best Artistic Contribution Award. He also directed the 2006 documentary “Lake of Fire.”

	The release of “American History X” was famously fraught. Kaye fell out with New Line Cinema and Norton over the edit, and the version that reached theaters, which Norton had a hand in cutting, ran longer than Kaye’s original 95-minute cut. Kaye spent around $100,000 on dozens of ads in the Hollywood trades, Variety among them, some of which attacked Norton and the studio. The Directors Guild of America turned down his request to swap his directing credit for a pseudonym, among them “Humpty Dumpty.” Kaye later sued the guild and New Line for $200 million, a case that was dismissed in 2000.

	Kaye returned to the saga in “Humpty Dumpty X,” a 74-minute documentary built from camcorder footage he shot during the dispute, including phone calls with studio executives. The film, which also features Marlon Brando, world premiered in the Spotlight Documentary section of this year’s Tribeca Festival.

	Outside of features, Kaye built a reputation in music videos and commercials. His ad work spans Nike’s “Kick It,” Volvo’s “Twister,” Dunlop’s “Tested for the Unexpected,” a run of InterCity campaigns for British Rail and the “Furry Friends” spot for solid fuel.

schema.headline: ‘American History X’ Director Tony Kaye Takes On Leicester’s Giant Monsters in Short ‘Will You Still Love Me Tomorrow?’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Shah Rukh Khan, Kajol, Rani Mukerji, Salman Khan Starrer ‘Kuch Kuch Hota Hai’ to Mark 30th Anniversary at Edinburgh Film Festival With Karan Johar
description: “Kuch Kuch Hota Hai,” Karan Johar’s first film as director, starring Shah Rukh Khan, Kajol and Rani Mukerji, will screen at the Edinburgh Internati
body:
“Kuch Kuch Hota Hai,” Karan Johar’s first film as director, starring Shah Rukh Khan, Kajol and Rani Mukerji, will screen at the Edinburgh International Film Festival in 2028 to celebrate its 30th anniversary, with Johar set to attend.

	Johar received the invitation earlier this week at a meeting he hosted at the Mumbai offices of his banner, Dharma Productions, with Scotland’s First Minister John Swinney and David Smith, interim executive director of Screen Scotland. The talks centered on Scotland as a location and partner for Indian film and TV, covering production and co-production as well as talent development and cultural exchange.
	

	“It was a pleasure to meet Karan Johar in Mumbai, and I am delighted that he has accepted the Edinburgh International Film Festival’s invitation to celebrate the 30th anniversary of ‘Kuch Kuch Hota Hai’ which holds a special place in the hearts of communities across Scotland and beyond. I look forward to welcoming him to Edinburgh,” Swinney said.

	Swinney added that during his India trip he had met with members of the country’s film industry, Dharma among them, about future collaboration. “Scotland’s screen industry has tremendous potential as a creative partner for Indian film and television, offering the infrastructure, expertise and world-class filming locations to support a wide range of productions,” he said.

	In the film, widower Rahul (Khan) is steered by his young daughter back toward Anjali (Kajol), the college best friend who quietly loved him before he married Tina (Mukerji), while Salman Khan plays Anjali’s fiancé.
	

	No major Indian production before “Kuch Kuch Hota Hai” had shot as widely in Scotland. Johar’s unit filmed at Eilean Donan Castle, Glen Coe, Tantallon Castle and Inchmahome Priory, and the Scottish scenery became central to the film’s look. The film went on to forge a lasting link between the country’s landscapes and mainstream Indian cinema.

	Other guests will also join the anniversary screening. Dates for the 2028 edition have yet to be announced.

	“At EIFF we are always thinking about the future and what’s next. So we jumped at an opportunity like this, to plant the seeds for a celebration of a legendary, much-loved film at our festival, a film featuring Scotland and some of the most iconic stars of Bollywood cinema on screen. We can’t wait for what promises to be something truly special for our 81st edition in 2028. But in the meantime, watch this space for more news of our 80th next August,” said EIFF CEO and festival director Paul Ridd.

	Before then, the festival will celebrate its 80th anniversary when it runs Aug. 12–18, 2027. Submissions for that edition open in January, and more details will follow in the coming months.

	The milestone edition follows the festival’s revival in 2024 under Ridd and festival producer Emma Boa. EIFF is backed by Screen Scotland.

schema.headline: Shah Rukh Khan, Kajol, Rani Mukerji, Salman Khan Starrer ‘Kuch Kuch Hota Hai’ to Mark 30th Anniversary at Edinburgh Film Festival With Karan Johar

title: Japan’s Anime Market Hits Record $28.2 Billion as Local Sales Surge
description: Spending on Japanese anime worldwide reached a record JPY4.45 trillion ($28.2 billion) in 2025. That is up 15.8% on the previous year, and overseas
body:
Spending on Japanese anime worldwide reached a record JPY4.45 trillion ($28.2 billion) in 2025. That is up 15.8% on the previous year, and overseas consumers now account for well over half of the total.

	Hasegawa Masahiro, editor-in-chief of the Association of Japanese Animations’ (AJA) annual “Anime Industry Report,” presented the preliminary figures Friday at TIFFCOM, the market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival. The final numbers will appear in the 2026 edition of the report when it is published in December.
	

	The rate of growth was also a record, edging past the 15.7% posted in 2024. Overseas revenue climbed 17.2% to JPY2.54 trillion ($16.1 billion), while the local market grew 14.1% to JPY1.91 trillion ($12.1 billion). The overseas share of the total rose to 57.1% from 56.5% a year earlier.

	Much of the gain came from home. Local growth was 4.6% in 2024, based on revised figures for 2023, while overseas growth slowed from the 26% recorded that year.

	For years, a sluggish home market sat alongside rapid growth abroad. Hasegawa said 2025 broke that pattern, with both sides growing strongly. Overseas revenue first overtook local revenue in 2023, and the gap has widened every year since. He cautioned that exchange rates and global conditions affect the comparison. He added that the overseas total reflects a range of market factors, not only how well individual titles travel.

	The AJA measures the business two ways. The broad figure estimates what consumers spend on everything connected to anime, from TV, film and streaming to merchandise, music and live events. A narrower measure tracks revenue earned by animation studios themselves. That studio figure rose 8.4% to a record JPY505.5 billion ($3.2 billion), a slightly slower pace than the 9.1% growth of 2024.
	

	Overseas business made up 27.9% of studio revenue, up from 25.5% in 2024. Studios do not always deal directly with international partners, Hasegawa noted, which keeps that share relatively low.

	“The idea of studios holding the rights to their own works and managing them to generate revenue is growing year by year,” he said.

	Hasegawa pointed to Japanese titles placing high at the box office in various territories and on global streaming charts. “Just last week, I saw a report that a Japanese anime was No. 2 globally,” he said. “I believe the breakthrough has truly been achieved.”

	Japanese anime make up 100 of the 300 TV series with the most user votes on IMDb, including nine of the top 20. “Attack on Titan” leads the ranking with 726,000 votes, ahead of “Rick and Morty.” “Death Note” is No. 3 and “One Piece” No. 9. The other Japanese titles in the top 20 are “Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood,” “Demon Slayer,” “One-Punch Man,” “Naruto Shippuden,” “Jujutsu Kaisen” and “Hunter x Hunter.”

	The data feeds into a government target for content exports of JPY20 trillion ($126.9 billion) in overseas sales by 2033, with anime expected to contribute JPY6 trillion ($38.1 billion). Japanese content earned JPY6.1 trillion ($38.7 billion) abroad in 2024, and anime accounted for roughly one-third of that.

	In the report’s survey, studios listed two priorities for growth markets: localization fitted to local language, culture and law, and anti-piracy measures.

	At home, Hasegawa said, anime has long worked as a driver for related content, goods and services. Abroad, it has so far succeeded mainly as something to watch, and the next phase is selling merchandise and services to fans worldwide. He singled out family anime, which is recognized across generations in Japan, as a category whose wide reach at home could become merchandising sales abroad.

	“By taking the structure that has been built up in Japan overseas, I believe we can grow toward the JPY6 trillion target,” Hasegawa said.

	Ishikawa Kazuko, who heads both the AJA and Nippon Animation, opened the session.

	“Above all, it is essential that we build a better environment in which the creators who make the works, and everyone involved in production management, can devote themselves to creating with peace of mind,” Ishikawa said.

schema.headline: Japan’s Anime Market Hits Record $28.2 Billion as Local Sales Surge

title: Rishab Shetty’s Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Epic ‘The Pride of Bharat’ Lands T-Series, Set as Two-Part Saga (EXCLUSIVE)
description: India’s T-Series has boarded “The Pride of Bharat – Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj,” Sandeep Singh’s historical epic starring “Kantara” actor Rishab S
body:
India’s T-Series has boarded “The Pride of Bharat – Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj,” Sandeep Singh’s historical epic starring “Kantara” actor Rishab Shetty as the Maratha king. 

	The project will now be made in two parts, and filming begins in early 2027.

	Bhushan Kumar and Krishan Kumar will produce for T-Series Films, and Shetty also comes on as a co-producer. To mark the partnership, Bhushan Kumar presented Shetty with a century-old painting of the Maratha ruler.
	

	Shetty wrote, directed and starred in “Kantara,” the 2022 Kannada-language hit that won him the Indian National Film Award for best actor. Its prequel, “Kantara: Chapter 1,” was released in 2025 and grossed more than $91 million worldwide.

	Shetty and Singh first announced the film in December 2024. 

	Across the two films, the saga will follow Shivaji Maharaj through his major battles and victories, the sacrifices that came with them and episodes from his life that are less widely known. The story centers on his skill as a military strategist, his leadership and his idea of Swarajya.

	The production will have a large ensemble cast. Its creative team combines talent from India and abroad.

	“Maharashtra and Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj have given us a legacy to be proud of, and I believe it is our responsibility to honor that legacy through cinema and share it with the world,” Bhushan Kumar said. “When Sandeep Singh narrated ‘The Pride of Bharat – Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj,’ I felt a deep sense of responsibility to bring this extraordinary story to the big screen.”
	

	Kumar cited Shetty’s screen presence and his ability to bring legendary figures to life, adding that he believes the team is the right combination “to bring the courage, vision and spirit of Swarajya to audiences across generations. For T-Series, this is more than a film; it is a tribute to Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj and his timeless legacy.”

	Shivaji founded the Maratha kingdom in 17th-century western India and spent much of his life fighting the Mughal Empire. He is revered in Maharashtra and a frequent subject for Indian filmmakers. Recent films about him and his circle include “Tanhaji: The Unsung Warrior” (2020), the Marathi film “Har Har Mahadev” (2022) and “Chhaava” (2025), which centered on his son Sambhaji. In May, Riteish Deshmukh directed “Raja Shivaji” and starred in it as the king. Released in the Hindi and Marathi languages, it became the highest-grossing Marathi film of all time.

	Pre-production is under way ahead of the 2027 shoot.

	Singh co-wrote the film with Rishi Virmani. Gulshan Kumar and T-Series Films present the project, which Legend Studios produces alongside T-Series Films. Shiv Chanana and Kabiir Sadanand join Shetty as co-producers.

schema.headline: Rishab Shetty’s Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Epic ‘The Pride of Bharat’ Lands T-Series, Set as Two-Part Saga (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Gay Filipino Couple’s Homecoming Documentary ‘We Had a Plan’ Boarded by Cat&Docs Ahead of IDFA Premiere, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “We Had a Plan,” a documentary about a gay Filipino couple who head home after a decade as undocumented cleaners in the Netherlands, has been picke
body:
“We Had a Plan,” a documentary about a gay Filipino couple who head home after a decade as undocumented cleaners in the Netherlands, has been picked up for international sales by Paris-based Cat&Docs ahead of its world premiere at IDFA. 

	Variety has the exclusive first look at the trailer.

	Directed by Suzanne Raes and co-directed by Venice De Castro Atienza, the film will bow in the Luminous strand of the International Documentary Festival Amsterdam, which runs Nov. 12-22. It is also in the running for IDFA’s Best Dutch Film Award.
	

	Paul and Daniel spent 10 years cleaning in the Netherlands without papers before moving back to the Philippines, where their relatives now regard them as rich. They arrive with big ideas for the life ahead of them. Money and optimism only go so far, though. As the savings from their years abroad run down, and the limits on their freedom as a gay couple close in, the relationship comes under strain.

	“We shaped this film into a bittersweet love story about a couple whose relationship is tested by global inequalities in wealth, social security and acceptance of queer people,” Raes said. “It reveals the sacrifices migrant workers make to achieve their goals, humanizing an often invisible workforce.”

	De Castro Atienza said that Paul and Daniel, after 12 years away with no way of going back, had gambled everything on a better future for themselves and their family. “As a Filipino filmmaker who has also left my home country, I approach their story with closeness and intimacy, recognizing the collective experience of choosing between leaving to provide for loved ones and staying to share a life with them. In ‘We Had a Plan,’ we witness two people try to change the configuration of the world to build a place for their love.”
	

	Catherine Le Clef, president and CEO of Cat&Docs, said the company had responded straight away to the warmth of the film and its likable protagonists. “Through their personal stories, the film offers a deeply human perspective on a foreign workforce that is too often reduced to statistics, stereotypes or simply made invisible. It is also an important reminder of the very real human cost behind the systems that depend on their labor. We felt that this combination of intimacy, tenderness and social relevance made the film particularly powerful and timely.”

	Raes’ earlier films include “Close to Vermeer” (2023) and “Where Dragons Live” (2024), the latter earning her a BAFTA Scotland nomination. De Castro Atienza’s first feature, “Last Days at Sea” (2021), debuted at the Berlinale and went on to Visions du Réel, Hot Docs and IDFA.

	Ilja Roomans produced for Dutch outfit Docmakers, with Alemberg Ang co-producing for the Philippines’ Daluyong Studios. De Castro Atienza executive produced through Svemirko Film Productions. Cinema Delicatessen will handle distribution in the Netherlands.

	Watch the trailer here:

schema.headline: Gay Filipino Couple’s Homecoming Documentary ‘We Had a Plan’ Boarded by Cat&Docs Ahead of IDFA Premiere, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Annecy Winner ‘The Violinist’ Found Its Italian Co-Producers at Tokyo Market, Director Ervin Han Tells Anime Co-Production Panel
description: A meeting at TIFFCOM in 2023 brought Italian co-producers to “The Violinist,” the animated feature that went on to win the top prize at France’s An
body:
A meeting at TIFFCOM in 2023 brought Italian co-producers to “The Violinist,” the animated feature that went on to win the top prize at France’s Annecy International Animation Film Festival this year, Singaporean filmmaker Ervin Han told a panel at the Tokyo market.

	Han, co-founder and CEO of Singapore’s Robot Playground Media, spoke at “Anime’s New Frontier: Structuring & Financing International Co-Productions,” a session at TIFFCOM, the content market of the Tokyo International Film Festival. Speakers agreed that international anime co-productions work best when overseas partners are involved early, with financing, deal structures and rights management considered from development through release. Kawano Masao, program manager at Into Global, moderated.
	

	Han co-directed and produced “The Violinist.” On his first TIFFCOM visit, he met Italian producer Cristiano Bortone and his team at Altri Occhi, who later joined the film as co-producers. This year, Han returned as producer to pitch “A Banquet for Hungry Ghosts,” an animated feature about food, horror and temptation, with partners from Singapore, Taiwan, Malaysia and Ireland.

	Han described “The Violinist” as a story of friendship over a decade. The film itself also took 10 years from conception to completion. “With different roles in my projects, I find promotion is even more challenging than production,” he said.

	Ilan Urroz, CEO of France’s Foliascope, said co-production itself was nothing new and stressed the importance of platform partnerships, pointing to France’s investment obligations for streaming services. Under French rules, streamers must put at least 20% of the revenue they earn in France into European or French-language original film and audiovisual production, rising to 25% for some services that offer films within 12 months of their theatrical release. The rule applies to animation as well as other genres. Urroz named Netflix, Disney+, Crunchyroll, Prime Video and HBO Max as the leading platforms in France.
	

	Sakurai Taiki, CEO of Salamander Inc., drew on more than 25 years in anime and over 100 titles to stress the importance of people and talent. “Partners are the key to success,” he said.

	Asked how to find co-production partners, Urroz said, “Be creative, and don’t forget that every project is also a journey of a group of people.”

schema.headline: Annecy Winner ‘The Violinist’ Found Its Italian Co-Producers at Tokyo Market, Director Ervin Han Tells Anime Co-Production Panel

title: Mohammad Rasoulof, Shahrbanoo Sadat Push Back on Idea of Separate Oscar Category for Exiled Filmmakers as Cate Blanchett’s Displacement Film Fund Hits Tokyo
description: Iranian filmmaker Mohammad Rasoulof and Iranian-born Afghan director Shahrbanoo Sadat pushed back on the idea of a standalone Oscar category for ex
body:
Iranian filmmaker Mohammad Rasoulof and Iranian-born Afghan director Shahrbanoo Sadat pushed back on the idea of a standalone Oscar category for exiled filmmakers, speaking at the Tokyo International Film Festival as Cate Blanchett’s Displacement Film Fund gave its first five short films their Japan premiere.

	The question followed the Academy’s recent rule change making exiled filmmakers eligible for the Oscars. The Academy’s top leadership was present at the festival this week.
	

	“I really do not like to be labeled, and even this label is displaced, you know, because I’m not seeing myself like I’m Shahrbanoo Sadat, the displaced filmmaker. This is funny, this is a joke to me,” said Sadat, whose fund-backed short is “Super Afghan Gym.” “I’m not sure if I would love to be in the category of displaced, even if they give me the Oscar.”

	Rasoulof, who directed the fund’s “The Sense of Water,” said that as a filmmaker he wanted to put all his energy into making films, and that from that point of view it might not matter much where they are shown. “If there are certain specific categories, then sometimes those could cause an issue, so I would really like to focus my efforts on closing the distance and being closer,” he said.

	Clare Stewart, managing director of International Film Festival Rotterdam (IFFR), whose Hubert Bals Fund manages the Displacement Film Fund, pointed out that Rasoulof’s own “The Seed of the Sacred Fig,” nominated in the last Oscar cycle, was one of the first films to benefit from the change, and that it represented Germany.
	

	“And then what does that mean? What dialogue does that create? How does that open up our thinking more broadly about what the position of a displaced filmmaker or refugee filmmaker is in our social fabric?” Stewart said. “So I personally don’t feel there’s a need.”

	Blanchett, the fund’s co-founder, said everyone on the panel had welcomed the Academy’s ruling and the way it acknowledged the real situation facing artists around the world. “There’s so many wars and conflicts, and people displaced through no fault of their own, and often careers, artistic careers are interrupted. So the fact that the Academy is recognizing that, I think is, it sounds like a small thing, but it is very profound,” she said.

	The first cohort’s films have already had an Academy qualifying screening in Los Angeles, Blanchett said, with another set for New York in mid-November. “Of course for Academy considerations, but first and foremost so that yet another territory, the American territory, can see these extraordinary films,” she said.

	“I don’t want to be too trivial, but the film industry is very used to international co-productions,” Blanchett added. “The cultural diplomacy that happens within our own industry, I wish a lot of governments would model the same level of communication.”

	The fund backs filmmakers who are displaced themselves or who have a track record of telling authentic stories about displacement. It took shape at the UNHCR’s Global Refugee Forum in December 2023, where Blanchett, a UNHCR goodwill ambassador for more than a decade, first met Yanai Koji, a director and senior executive officer at Uniqlo parent Fast Retailing.

	“When one in 70 people around the world is displaced, Koji-san and I and the other people at the Refugee Forum, including UNHCR, were saying, why aren’t these stories more in the mainstream? Why aren’t we talking about them? And it’s a chance to dispel the toxic narrative that is often around displaced persons’ experience,” Blanchett said.

	Stewart said the effort gathered pace in October 2024, when she told Blanchett about the Hubert Bals Fund, which IFFR has run for 30 years to support filmmakers in countries where infrastructure is thin or where getting a film backed is politically difficult. IFFR signed on to manage the new fund, which launched at the festival in January 2025. Its founding partners are Yanai’s production company Mastermind, Uniqlo, the Tama Family Foundation, the Amahoro Coalition and Dutch foundation Droom en Daad. The Spinoza Foundation came aboard as a main partner at IFFR this year.
	

	The first cohort, unveiled at Cannes in 2025, comprises Rasoulof, Sadat, Mo Harawe, Hassan Fazili and Maryna Er Gorbach. Their films premiered at IFFR in January and have also screened in London and El Gouna, with São Paulo on the festival run as well. A second cohort is now making its films. Blanchett said the filmmakers were given full freedom over subject and point of view, and their stories did not have to address displacement directly.

	“The Sense of Water” centers on a migrant’s solitude and the struggle to learn a new language. “Three years ago, I had no choice but to flee my hometown and seek refuge overseas. There I had a sense of isolation, and I began to question this sense of isolation, wanting to understand where that would come from,” Rasoulof said.

	Sadat was born in Iran to parents who fled the Soviet-Afghan War in 1979, moved at age 11 to a small village in central Afghanistan, and was evacuated to France and then Germany when Afghanistan collapsed. The fund approached her while she was editing “No Good Men,” a romantic comedy in which she ended up playing the lead after her actor withdrew three weeks before the shoot. That film opened the Berlin Film Festival and is set for release in Japan next year.

	“I wanted to talk about these feelings of not being comfortable in your first and last home: your body,” Sadat said of “Super Afghan Gym.”

	Japanese star Yakusho Koji, Cannes best actor winner for “Perfect Days,” a collaborator on Uniqlo’s Peace for All charity T-shirt project, was the surprise guest at a post-screening talk and described “The Sense of Water” as “a very quiet, calm film about love and hardships and deep hurt.” Sadat’s gym-set film, he said, “really brought a smile to my face.” Sadat said she only realized the film was being read as a comedy when critics called it one after its Rotterdam premiere.

	Blanchett had a question of her own for Yakusho: “When are we going to work together?”

schema.headline: Mohammad Rasoulof, Shahrbanoo Sadat Push Back on Idea of Separate Oscar Category for Exiled Filmmakers as Cate Blanchett’s Displacement Film Fund Hits Tokyo

title: Taiwanese Feature ‘Uncle’ Wins Top Prize at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market Awards
description: Taiwanese project “Uncle,” directed by Yen Hao-hsuan, won the Tokyo Project Award on Friday at the seventh Tokyo Gap-Financing Market (TGFM) in Tok
body:
Taiwanese project “Uncle,” directed by Yen Hao-hsuan, won the Tokyo Project Award on Friday at the seventh Tokyo Gap-Financing Market (TGFM) in Tokyo.

	“Uncle” had already picked up the Asian Gen-Z Award earlier in the ceremony. Prizes went to a handful of the 24 projects selected for this year’s market.

	Yen’s debut feature, set in rural Taiwan between 1997 and 2000, follows a boy whose devotion to his uncle, a man with an intellectual disability, turns to shame as he grows up and leaves home. The story draws on Yen’s own 18 years living with his uncle. The film is produced by Flash Forward Entertainment founder Patrick Mao Huang, whose credits include Cannes Critics’ Week Grand Prize winner “Tiger Stripes,” and Sung Chin-hsuan. The project made its first Asian market outing at the Busan Asian Project Market earlier this month.
	

	Jury member Nam Jongsuk, a programmer at the Bucheon International Fantastic Film Festival and managing director of the Network of Asian Fantastic Films (NAFF), said “this project looks at society and bravely goes against prejudices, without sugarcoating the subject.” The jury hoped Yen would deliver something “uncompromising,” he added.

	Yen said he hadn’t expected the win. “I’ll take this as the energy to shoot and finish the film,” he said.

	Now in its second year, the Asian Gen-Z Award carries a JPY500,000 ($3,300) prize. The winner is chosen by a committee of five film students from universities and graduate programs, who pick a project that appeals to people aged 20 to 28.

	“Above all, the jury recognized this as a story that demands to be told right now,” the students said of “Uncle,” adding that the film was “resisting simplistic emotional appeals.”
	

	Japanese-Canadian co-production “Wild Zero Overdrive,” from Takegei Company Limited, won the White Light Post-Production Award. The prize comes with $25,000 in post-production services from Thailand-based White Light studio. Directed by Takeuchi Tetsuro, the film is a follow-up to his 1999 cult film “Wild Zero” and stars the real-life punk band Guitar Wolf, who headlined the original. There was no acceptance speech, but winners and presenters alike yelled “rock and roll!” in the spirit of the project.

	“Wild Zero Overdrive” came to Tokyo through the Frontières fiction feature selection, part of TIFFCOM’s first partnership with the co-production market of Canada’s Fantasia International Film Festival.

	Brazilian feature “Nature Boy,” directed by Matias Mariani and produced by Primo Filmes, won the Mellow Tunes Sound Design Award. The prize offers in-kind sound design services valued at up to $10,000 from Thailand’s Mellow Tunes.

	TIFFCOM managing director Ikeda Kaori hosted the ceremony. Nam sat on the jury alongside Meiske Taurisia, a producer at Palari Films, and Paolo Bertolin, a consultant for the Venice Film Festival.

	The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival.

schema.headline: Taiwanese Feature ‘Uncle’ Wins Top Prize at Tokyo Gap-Financing Market Awards

title: Shabana Azmi, Marco Müller Set for Inaugural Kathmandu Film Festival
description: Veteran Indian actor Shabana Azmi and film critic and historian Marco Müller are among the guests at the first Kathmandu Film Festival (KFF), which
body:
Veteran Indian actor Shabana Azmi and film critic and historian Marco Müller are among the guests at the first Kathmandu Film Festival (KFF), which runs Oct. 30–Nov. 1 in Nepal.

	Launched by Kathmandu Metropolitan City, the three-day event will screen 40 films from 14 countries across several strands: the International Panorama, Nepal Panorama Shorts, a program of restored Nepali features and open-air screenings. Filmmakers and artists from around Asia are also due to attend. The city, a UNESCO Creative City of Film, set up the festival to showcase Nepali and international independent cinema and to build cultural ties.
	

	Marine Atlan’s Cannes premiere “La Gradiva” is among the international selections, as is Shahrbanoo Sadat’s “No Good Men,” which debuted in Berlin this year.

	“The international panorama is a curated showcase of global, contemporary and independent cinema that represents powerful stories, unique voices and distinct cultural perspectives,” said Ramyata Limbu, KFF’s artistic director. “The Nepal panorama shorts feature diverse and compelling stories about Nepal by emerging local talent.”

	Nepal’s film history gets a section of its own. A retrospective of restored titles from the 1970s and 1980s includes “Kumari,” credited as the country’s first color feature.

	Yamagata, Japan, which holds the same UNESCO film designation as Kathmandu, is the focus of a separate shorts program. Organizers tied the showcase to the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Nepal and Japan, and said it is meant to deepen links between the two cities.
	

	Events are spread across venues including Basantapur, City Hall, the Nepal Tourism Board, Jai Nepal Cinema and Taragaon. Alongside the films, the lineup takes in a heritage walk, master classes and conversations with filmmakers, with prizes to be handed out in the youth video challenge and Nepal panorama sections. Screenings are free, though some events require booking ahead.

	“Kathmandu is not just the city of its indigenous communities, whose culture and heritage are at its heart. It is also a city shaped by people from every corner of Nepal,” said Sunita Dangol, Kathmandu’s acting mayor. “Over generations, communities from across the country have brought their traditions, languages, art, music and stories to Kathmandu. That coming together is what makes this city so vibrant and unique.”

	Organizers are pitching KFF as a festival for the general public, one that links the city’s heritage with present-day cinema and the global film community.

	“Nepal has been through a profound tragedy with the floods, and in moments like these, stories become even more important,” Dangol said. “They help us make sense of what we have experienced, connect with one another, heal and find the courage to move forward.”

schema.headline: Shabana Azmi, Marco Müller Set for Inaugural Kathmandu Film Festival

title: Sir Ian McKellen Mourns the Loss of Sir Patrick Stewart
description:
Sir Ian McKellen
                          Shares Touching Tribute to Sir Patrick Stewart
body:
Sir Ian McKellen
                          Shares Touching Tribute to Sir Patrick Stewart
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 29, 2026
                            5:55 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sir Ian McKellen was hit hard by the death of his close friend and collaborator, Sir Patrick Stewart ... mourning the loss of a legend.
      
    
            Ian remembered his friend saying, "He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The 'Lord of the Rings' star remembered meeting Patrick "half a century ago" ... however, his first strong memory of his friend was warning him not to take his now iconic 'Star Trek' -- believing it would put his prestigious stage career at risk.
      

            Ian went on to express gratitude on behalf of the "Trekkies" and "film and theatre audiences" who were able to marvel at his late friend's talents. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The iconic actors' friendship spans decades -- they both starred in "X-Men" together back in 2000.
      
    
            Ian even officiated Patrick's wedding to Sunny Ozell in a Mexican restaurant back in 2013.
      
    
            Patrick previously recalled the sweet, spontaneous ceremony on "Jimmy Kimmel Live!," saying ... "We learned that [McKellen] could not use his [ministry] credentials in Nevada, which is where we were getting married … so we invited Ian and two of our guests and a [theater] director to a Mexican restaurant for dinner."
      
    
            As we previously reported, Patrick passed away at 86 following a brief battle with Alzheimer's.

title: NYC Driver Plows Through Halloween Event, Injuring Several People
description:
NYC Driver
                          Plows Sedan Into Halloween Event ...
body:
NYC Driver
                          Plows Sedan Into Halloween Event ...
                          Multiple People Injured
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A driver in New York City hopped a curb and plowed into a Halloween event hosted by the NYPD ... injuring several people, including a child.
      
    
            The driver -- who New York Post reports is a 56-year-old man -- allegedly lost control of a black sedan and ran directly into a "Trunk or Treat" event Thursday outside the 83rd Precinct Station House in Brooklyn.
      
    
            Authorities told the outlet he also struck a private ambulance that was on scene in case of emergency.
      

        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Reports differ ... with the New York Post noting 4 people -- including a child -- were injured, while CBS says 6 people sustained injuries. First responders checked on several others at the scene as well.
      
    
            Photos and video from the scene show the street corner thrown into chaos ... and the damaged ambulance.
      
    
            NYP reports the driver was taken into police custody ... and a breathalyzer test has been administered.
      
    
            Unclear exactly what caused the incident ... but the Post's sources are clear that a terrorist attack is not suspected at this time.
